title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12)
hookLine: a servant despised, wounded, bearing others' griefs; Christians see Jesus here, Jewish readers often Israel

lines: A CHARIOT ON THE GAZA ROAD.
cards: A chariot is rolling slowly down the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. In it sits an official of the queen of Ethiopia, her treasurer, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem.
He's reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah. A man named Philip runs up alongside and hears him. In the King James words of Acts, Philip asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?"
How can I, the official says, unless someone guides me? Then he asks what people have asked about this passage ever since: "of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?"

teach.b: Isaiah describes a figure he calls the servant. Not handsome, not impressive; people look away from him. In the King James Bible: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."
Then the voice in the poem, a we, has a shock of realization.
We thought he was being punished by God. We were wrong. "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows."
And: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."
Stripes are the marks of a whip; the healing comes through his wounds. "All we like sheep have gone astray." He is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open his mouth.
And yet the poem ends with him lifted up, seeing light. So, the Ethiopian's question: who is he? Christians, from the beginning, have answered: Jesus.
In Acts, Philip starts from this very passage and tells the official about Jesus, and the official asks to be baptized in the next water they pass.
The New Testament echoes these lines again and again, and many churches read them on Good Friday.

Jewish interpreters have most often read the servant as Israel itself, a people suffering among the nations, since Isaiah elsewhere calls Israel my servant; some have read him as the prophet, or a righteous few.
Both readings are old, and both are held seriously.

teach.h: WITH HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED.
teach.b: And among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a nearly complete copy of Isaiah, made well before Jesus was born, with this chapter in it.

how: Christians read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 on Good Friday in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and many Protestant churches, and lines from it are sung in Handel's Messiah and in many Passion hymns.

games.q: you're the Ethiopian official, reading a scroll you don't understand, and a stranger offers to explain. what do you do?
o: say no thanks and keep reading.
invite him up into the chariot.

games.why: he invites Philip to sit with him, asks of whom speaketh the prophet this?, and by the end asks to be baptized at the next water.

practice: Bring to mind someone who carries other people's pain, a nurse, a caregiver, a parent sitting up with a sick child, a friend everyone calls in a crisis, and picture their shoulders, all they hold that nobody sees.
Stay with them a while without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for the strength they need tonight.
